question: What are good early weapon upgrades for the Driller in Deep Rock Galactic Survivor? Keep it to a short list.
answer:
Alright, listen up, you wanna know about those early weapon upgrades for the Driller? It ain't about grabbin' every shiny thing, mate. You gotta be smart.

First thing, you pick *one* weapon you wanna carry for the whole run. Don't try to be a jack-of-all-trades right out of the gate. That's a recipe for a messy end.

Second, once you pick that main weapon, you spend the rest of your upgrades on survivability. You want to make sure you don't get blown up by those Exploder bugs. Keep an eye on those upgrades and see what makes you tougher.

So, the short list is: Pick one weapon, then stack survivability. Simple as that.

notes.name: Nitra
notes.card:
Summary: The resource that pays for weapons rather than for your dwarf.
Uses: Buys weapon upgrade cards at the between-stage shop and rerolls the artifact choice from the Supply Pod.
Tips: No nitra means an underleveled weapon however much gold you mined, so keep mining it for whichever weapon carries the run.

notes.name: Upgrades and overclocks
notes.card: Levelling offers a choice of upgrades, and taking a little of everything is the common way to lose. Pick one weapon to carry the run and feed it, then spend the rest on survivability. Overclocks change what a weapon is for rather than making it bigger, so read what one removes as well as what it adds.

notes.name: Exploder
notes.card:
Summary: Large orange glyphids that walk into you and detonate in a wide blast.
Weak points: Fragile, and the blasts chain, so one popped early clears the group behind it.
Tips: Weapons fire themselves, so it dies where you stand - keep distance and the blast lands in the swarm instead.

question: black mesa how do i get across the electrified water
answer:
Alright, listen up, you wanna cross that electrified water? Don't be a mug and just stand there waiting for the current to stop. That water is straight-up lava, see? It’s constant shock damage until you get out or you’re toast. You gotta treat it like you’re wading through hot sludge, not some slow-motion puddle.

Here’s the skinny: don't try to time it. You gotta find something *above* the water. Look up! Desks, cabinets, shelves, those floating crates, even overhead pipes—anything that’s not submerged is your ticket across. If the gap is too wide to jump, don't sweat it; just grab those loose wooden crates and use 'em as stepping stones. Simple as that. Or, if you see a red wall switch or a breaker anywhere near the pool, cut the power. That’ll make the water safe for good.

notes.name: Starting out in Black Mesa
notes.card: Black Mesa is Half-Life rebuilt from the ground up on the Source engine, with new art, sound and voice work but the original's chapters, weapons and enemies kept on purpose rather than added to. The one exception is Xen: those chapters are mostly new work and far longer than the 1998 originals, so budget more time for the alien world than veterans remember. Expect the same shape of game throughout: no cutscenes, scripted scenes you walk through, a crowbar for crates and vents, and fights that go better from a doorway than from the middle of a room. There are 25 achievements, Workshop support and a separate deathmatch mode; the campaign itself is single-player only.

notes.name: The opening tram ride and where it leads
notes.card: Black Mesa opens with a long tram ride that needs no input beyond looking around; it carries you from the surface entrance through checkpoints and cargo bays into the underground facility, and doubles as an unskippable loading screen for the level ahead. Step off at the platform, badge through the checkpoint, and follow the corridor signs to the locker room, where you change into the orange HEV suit before the day's work — the path there is linear, so a door that will not open yet is one you have not reached the switch for. Anomalous Materials, the lab down the following hall, is where the real gameplay opens up: once things go wrong there, the crowbar on the floor nearby is the first weapon in the game, and from then on every locked vent or wooden crate is worth swinging at before hunting for another way around.

notes.name: Crossing the electrified waste pools
notes.card: The waste-treatment area has stretches of standing water with live wiring dropped into it, and the current is constant — there is no safe moment and no warning cycle to wait for. Stepping in deals continuous shock damage until you get out or die, so treat the flooded floor like lava rather than something to time. Cross on anything above the water: desks, cabinets, shelves, floating crates and overhead pipes all work, and the route is usually built into the room once you look up. Better still, cut the power — a red wall switch, breaker or lever, usually just outside the flooded area or at its far end, makes the water safe for good. Where a gap is too wide to jump, push or carry loose wooden crates into the water and use them as stepping stones.

notes.name: Starting out in Hollow Knight
notes.card: A side-scrolling metroidvania: a huge connected kingdom under the town of Dirtmouth that opens piece by piece as you find abilities. There is no map of an area until you find Cornifer, the humming cartographer, and buy his copy, and it only fills in as you rest at benches once you own a quill from his wife in Dirtmouth. Benches are everything: they save, restore your masks, and are the only place charms can be swapped. Your nail is short, so learn early to bounce off enemies and spikes with a downward slash. Hitting enemies fills the soul meter; hold Focus to spend it healing one mask at a time, or tap it for spells. Dying is not the end: your Shade waits where you fell, holding your Geo.

notes.name: Broken Vessel
notes.card: The infected husk shaped like you, far west in the Ancient Basin past a gap that needs the Crystal Heart. It dashes with slashes that cover most of the arena, flails its nail overhead, leaps to slam down and throw four arcs of infection, shakes out a cascade of blobs that covers nearly everything when its health gets low, and spawns weak balloons that drift at you. It is one of the few bosses that gets knocked back, so Vengeful Spirit can hit it twice; Desolate Dive during the cascade both damages it and keeps you safe. A longer nail (Mark of Pride or Longnail) matches its reach, and Defender's Crest quietly clears the balloons. Heal when it staggers, head weighed down and shaking.

notes.name: Watcher Knights
notes.card: Six armoured husks at the top of the Watcher's Spire, fought at most two at a time; a new one wakes twenty seconds after the last, or two together if you kill fast. Each does a double slash, rolls as a ball along the floor and bounces after you, and is immune to the nail while rolling (spells still land). Their only answer to attacks from above is that bouncing roll, so fight from the air and never let them corner you. Before the fight, break the hidden wall on the approach and cut the chandelier's support: it drops on the second husk from the left and you fight five instead of six. Quick Focus matters here; Desolate Dive with Shaman Stone kills one in three casts while keeping you untouchable.
